intro: To write behavior incident reports for students on a Mac, stick to what you saw and heard, in the order it happened. Build one template in Pages or Google Docs, dictate the rough draft, then check names and times before you file it. Below you will find what this costs, why it happens, and fixes you can start today.
tldr: Write only what you saw and heard. Leave out verdicts like defiant or rude.
Use one template with the same six fields for every incident.
Dictate the draft with fn or Edit > Start Dictation, then check every name and time.
No study times incident reports on their own. Measure your own week for a few weeks.
A small share of teachers files most referrals. Count yours once a month and compare.

blocks.text: What a behavior incident report needs to say

A behavior incident report has one job. It records what happened so the next adult can act on it. Write for a reader who was not in the room. That reader might be an assistant principal, a counselor, or a family member who asks for a copy. If they can see the moment from your page, the report did its job.
Most forms ask for the same core facts. Keep them in this order, and you will never hunt for a detail at the last minute.

items: Date, time, and class period
Location, such as the hallway, the cafeteria line, or your room
Activity, such as independent reading or a group task
What the student did, in observable words
What the student said, in quotes when you can
What you did and what you said, in order
What happened next, including whether the student returned to class
Who else saw it or was told

blocks.text: Observable words separate a useful report from a label. 'He was disrespectful' tells the reader what you think. 'He called the worksheet stupid, then turned it face down' tells the reader what happened. Use verbs you could film. If a sentence needs a camera to check it, it belongs in the report.
A template you can copy into Pages or Google Docs

Build the template once, then reuse it. Open a new document in Pages or Google Docs and add one heading for each field. Save a clean master copy, and duplicate it for every incident. The [Pages routine for teachers](/for/teachers/pages) and the [Google Docs guide for teachers](/for/teachers/google-docs) both cover the basics.

rows: Threw a pencil at the desk beside them
What the class was doing just before
What you said or did, in order
Asked once to stop, then moved the seat
What the student said or did next
Said I'm not doing this, then put head down
What happens next, and who knows
Finished the task at the end of class, counselor emailed
Whether and when the family was contacted
Not yet. Will call after school per team plan
blocks.caption: Field examples for a short incident report. Use codes or initials where your district requires it.

blocks.text: Use initials or a code if your district asks for it. Some schools keep the full name only in their official system. Check before you type a full name into a personal document, a form, or an AI tool.
A worked example, from scribbled notes to a clean report

Start with the mess. Your notes might read: 'Student B, shouting, cut line, said nobody cares, left room, came back after bell, apologized.' That is enough to write from. Put the facts in the order they happened, and drop the labels.

The clean version reads like this. During the move to lunch, Student B walked to the front of the line and ignored the line order. When I asked them to go to the back, they said nobody cares and left the room. Student B came back after the bell and apologized. I held a short check-in before the next class. No further action was taken.
Notice what changed. The labels disappeared. The sequence stayed. The follow-up is on the page, so the next adult knows what already happened and does not have to ask.
Edge cases that change the report
Some incidents need more care than a standard template gives. Check these cases before you write.

items: Student with an IEP or behavior plan: read the plan first and note which supports were in place.
Safety incident: follow your school's safety procedure first. Write the report after the student is safe and supervised.
Repeat incidents: keep a running log, so each new report shows the pattern, not only the latest event.
Two adults saw it: name both, and note who wrote which part. Do not merge their words into one quote.
Student denies it: write what the student said, in quotes. Then write what you saw. Do not add a conclusion.
Sensitive home information: do not write what you heard about a family unless you saw it or policy requires it. Ask your counselor.

blocks.text: The IEP and behavior plan case matters most. If a plan exists, the report should show whether the plan's steps happened. The IES practice guide says to draw on colleagues and families when you address behavior problems, and it rates that moderate. For the wider IEP paperwork, see the [IEP goals routine for teachers](/for/teachers/problems/draft-iep-goals-faster-special-education).
Mistakes that make reports weaker

items: Writing a verdict instead of a fact, such as 'defiant' or 'out of control'.
Writing hours later, when you remember the feeling more than the words.
Naming other students who were not involved.
Adding sarcasm, humor, or venting. Those lines read badly to anyone who was not there.
Leaving out what happened before the incident. The lead-up often matters most.
Writing on a phone in a hallway where students or other adults can see the screen.
Treating the report as the whole response. A report records the event. It does not change it.

blocks.text: Try the read-aloud test. Read the report out loud, once, as if a stranger will ask about it. Any sentence that makes you want to say 'well, actually' needs a fact behind it.
Dictate the first draft, then check it

Typing the whole report takes time. Dictation can get a rough draft down fast. On a Mac, press the Microphone key or the Dictation shortcut. You can also choose Edit > Start Dictation. Apple says Keyboard settings show whether dictation is processed on the device or sent to Siri servers. Look there before you dictate anything about a student.

Dictation mishears names and dates. Read every name, time, and place before you save. Press ⌘F to find each name in the draft and check its spelling. Apple says its on-device model improves punctuation and capitalization on M3 or later Macs with at least 12GB of memory.

Lazur dictates the same way in any app. Hold fn, speak, and let go. Lazur types clean, formatted text at your cursor, so the draft lands in Pages or Google Docs. Add school terms to the personal dictionary so they come out right. Keep student names out of it unless your policy allows them.
Track patterns without a new system

A single report tells one story. Ten reports, read together, show a pattern. A simple Google Form can collect the basics for each incident. Responses save to a linked Google Sheet, so you can sort and count them later.

To choose the destination, open the form and go to Responses > Summary > More > Select destination for responses. Then create a new spreadsheet or pick an existing one. Google's help page says later permission changes to the form do not sync to the sheet. Check sharing on the sheet separately.

Keep the form short. Ask for date, class period, behavior type from a list, location, adult involved, and follow-up. Keep the full narrative in your template document. Link the two by date and a student code, if your policy allows it.
Where your own referral count fits the research

A study of 2,900 K-12 teachers at more than 100 urban California schools found that about 5 percent of teachers issued nearly 35 percent of office discipline referrals. The study was published in Education Researcher in 2023. Frequent referrers were mostly early-career teachers. The authors counted frequent referrers as those who issued 46 or more referrals in a school year.

A high count is not automatically a failing. It can mean you work in a hard room, or that you file reports for more events. Compare your count with your team, then look at what you can change. Referrals began falling at about three years of experience, so the pattern shifts with practice.

The same data show why wording matters. In the EdSurge write-up, Black students were 22% of students receiving referrals but 7% of district enrollment. The Black-to-white referral ratio rose from 1.6:1 to 3.4:1 once the top 5% of teachers were included. Precise, fair wording protects every student in the record.
What the research does and does not tell you

No study measures the time teachers spend on behavior incident reports. The Dutch audit timed general paperwork and did not break out behavior documentation. Treat the hours as background, not as a measurement of your own week.

The evidence on fixes is uneven. The IES What Works Clearinghouse practice guide rates modifying the classroom learning environment and teaching new skills as strong evidence. It rates identifying the specifics of problem behavior as moderate. That is the strongest support for the writing habit on this page.

Other evidence is thin. A 2023 randomized trial with 83 newly graduated teachers improved knowledge and self-efficacy, but it did not measure referrals. A mentoring program reported fewer out-of-class referrals, but the article gives no sample size or effect size.
Shortcuts and snippets for the parts you repeat

Shortcuts on a Mac can ask you questions and run a fixed set of steps. Open the Shortcuts app and add an Ask for Input action for each field. Then add a step that copies the result to the clipboard. Apple's Shortcuts guide says you can run a shortcut from the app, Siri, widgets, Spotlight, and Apple Watch.

Keep the shortcut dull. A prompt for the date, class period, behavior type, and adult's name is enough. A shortcut that writes the narrative for you tempts you to skip the facts. Ask Lazur to guide you through each step, one click at a time.
Lazur also has snippets. Save your template skeleton as a snippet, so the headings drop in with one phrase. Clipboard slots help when the same policy sentence belongs in several reports.
When the report goes to a family

A family may ask for the report, or you may need to call. Send a short factual summary in your own words, not the internal form. Write it as if the family will read it, because they may. Check district rules before you send any student information by email.

The routine for parent emails is in [how to reply to parent emails quickly on Mac](/for/teachers/problems/reply-parent-emails-quickly-teachers). The [Gmail page for teachers](/for/teachers/gmail) covers templates and shortcuts for the same job.
What Lazur does and does not do here

Lazur helps you think, write, and find things. It does not click buttons, fill in a form, or send an email for you. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to get an answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

That matters for student records. Hold the shortcut only when the screen shows nothing you cannot share under your policy. Lazur runs on macOS, and Windows is planned, not available. Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card, and you can compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing).
Practice the routine on a made-up example first. Once it feels routine, use it on a real incident. Check the output against your notes every time.

faq.question: Should I put student names in the report?
faq.answer: Follow your district's rules on student records. Some schools want full names in the official system only. If policy allows names in a personal document, still limit names to the people who need them. When in doubt, use initials and ask your administrator.

faq.question: How long should a behavior incident report be?
faq.answer: Long enough for the next reader to act on it, and no longer. If the form gives you one box, write a short paragraph in time order. Add detail only when it changes what happens next.

faq.question: How soon should I write the report?
faq.answer: Write it before you leave school, while the order of events is still clear. Memory keeps the feeling and loses the sequence. A short, factual draft beats a perfect report written days later.

faq.question: Does Lazur record my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Check your district's rules before you use any AI tool with student records.

faq.question: Can Lazur fill in my school's form for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It can dictate text at your cursor, explain what a field wants, and guide you through each click, one at a time.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available. You can start with a free trial with no credit card, and plan details are on the pricing page.

faq.question: Do I need a paid behavior system to write these reports?
faq.answer: No. The routine on this page needs a template, your Mac, and optionally a Google Form. Paid systems exist. SWIS lists at $500 per school per year on the PBIS Apps pricing page, which also has inconsistent discount labels, so confirm the price before you quote it.

faq.question: What if a student has a behavior plan?
faq.answer: Read the plan before you write. Note which steps you used and what happened when you used them. The report should show the plan in action, not replace it.

costs.title: Hours that add up on paperwork
costs.text: No study measures incident reports on their own. The closest figure covers all paperwork. Full-time primary teachers in a Dutch Court of Audit study spent 6 to 8 hours a week on paperwork. Teachers in the UK, Belgium and Australia spent just over 4 hours. Each special-needs pupil added about 15 minutes a week. A behavior report lands on top of that load, not in place of it.

costs.title: Paid time, in dollars
costs.text: The median pay for kindergarten and elementary teachers was $63,820 in May 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. That is about $30.68 an hour over 2,080 hours, calculated by dividing. One hour a week over 36 weeks comes to roughly $1,100 of paid time per teacher. Paid hours and real admin time can differ, so treat this as a rough guide.

costs.title: Burnout that paperwork feeds
costs.text: In the RAND 2025 survey, 53% of teachers reported burnout, down from 60% in 2024. Education Week lists administrative work among the main stressors, but it gives no percentage for that stressor. Paperwork is not the only cause. Still, a report written at the end of a long day adds weight to a week that already feels full.

costs.title: Weak reports slow down support
costs.text: A vague report gives the next adult less to work with. If the counselor cannot see what happened, the counselor has to ask you again. That costs both of you time, and it can delay the support the student needs. A clear report saves the follow-up conversation.

costs.title: Unequal outcomes when referrals cluster
costs.text: In the study data that EdSurge describes, Black students were 22% of students receiving referrals but 7% of district enrollment. The Black-to-white referral ratio rose from 1.6:1 to 3.4:1 once the top 5% of referring teachers were included. Your reports are part of that record. Precise, fair wording matters for every student in it.

causes.title: Writing from memory after a long day
causes.text: A report often gets written late in the day, or the next morning, from memory. Memory keeps the feeling and loses the sequence. The result is a summary, not a record. Summaries make the next reader guess what happened, and guessing takes time.

causes.title: Labels where the page needs facts
causes.text: A label such as disrespectful or out of control feels like a complete thought. It is not. The IES practice guide rates identifying the specifics of problem behavior as moderate evidence in elementary classrooms. Specific behavior is easier to act on, and labels hide the behavior a plan could change.

causes.title: A few teachers file most referrals
causes.text: A 2023 study in Education Researcher found that about 5% of teachers, mostly early-career, issued nearly 35% of office discipline referrals. Referrals began falling at about three years of experience. If you are new, the habit of writing facts is still forming. That is normal, and it is fixable.

causes.title: No shared model in the building
causes.text: A school may have a referral form but no examples. Each teacher then writes differently. One teacher writes four lines and another writes a page. Administrators receive reports that look nothing alike, so each one takes longer to read. A shared model of facts solves much of that without new software.

causes.title: Classroom conditions that the report cannot fix
causes.text: The IES practice guide rates modifying the classroom learning environment as strong evidence. It also rates teaching and reinforcing new skills as strong. A report records a symptom. The cause often sits in the room, in the routine, or in a skill the student never learned. If the report is the only response, the cycle repeats.

causes.title: Training gaps for newly graduated teachers
causes.text: A 2023 randomized trial with 83 newly graduated teachers tested behavior management training. It found gains in knowledge and self-efficacy, but not in the ability to analyze behavior management strategies. It did not measure referrals. Training helps, but a single course does not fix the daily paperwork load.

fixes.title: Use one template with the same fields
fixes.text: Pick six fields and use them every time. The fields are when, where, what the student did, what the student said, what you did, and what happened next. Write each field in observable words. Replace disrespectful with the words the student used, or with the action you saw. The same template makes every report easier to read and compare.

fixes.title: Write before you leave, while details hold
fixes.text: Set a fixed time to finish reports, such as before you pack up. Add a reminder with Apple Reminders if you need one. Write the sequence first and polish the wording second. A factual draft written the same day beats a polished one written later.

fixes.title: Dictate a rough draft, then check it
fixes.text: Speak the facts in order, one sentence each, into the template. On a Mac, press the Microphone key, use the Dictation shortcut, or choose Edit > Start Dictation. Then read every name, time, and place. Dictation is fast for a first draft. It is less reliable for names and numbers, so check those by eye.

fixes.title: Teach the skill, then write what you taught
fixes.text: The IES guide rates teaching and reinforcing new skills as strong evidence. Add one line to the report: which replacement skill you taught or reminded the student of. A report with a next step shows the plan is still active. It also gives the next adult a starting point.

fixes.title: Bring in colleagues and families early
fixes.text: The IES guide rates drawing on colleagues and families as moderate evidence. Tell your grade partner or counselor when a pattern starts, not after a long run of reports. Contact the family with a short, factual message. A quick call often helps more than another form.

fixes.title: Track patterns in a Google Form and Sheet
fixes.text: Make a Google Form with date, class period, behavior type, location, and follow-up. Open the form and go to Responses > Summary > More > Select destination for responses. Choose a new spreadsheet or an existing one. Use codes, not names, unless your district policy allows names in the sheet.

fixes.title: Compare your count with the research benchmark
fixes.text: A referral count means little until you have a comparison. The study that found about 5% of teachers issued nearly 35% of referrals defined frequent referrers as those with 46 or more in a school year. That cut-off is a research definition, not a rule for your school. Use it to start a conversation with your team.

plan.label: Today
plan.title: Set up one template
plan.text: Open Pages or Google Docs and make one document with headings for when, where, what the student did, what the student said, what you did, and what happened next. Save it as a master copy. Duplicate it for each incident, and keep names out of the master copy.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write every incident the same day
plan.text: Write before you leave school. Use the template and observable verbs. Dictate the draft if the report is long or your hands are busy. Save the file where your district says to keep it, and check the rules before you store anything.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check names and times
plan.text: Read the report aloud once. Look for verdicts and remove them. Press ⌘F to find each name, then check its spelling. Delete any name the report does not need.

plan.label: Week 1
plan.title: Start a simple log
plan.text: Build a Google Form with date, class period, behavior type, location, and follow-up. Go to Responses > Summary > More > Select destination for responses to choose a sheet. Use codes instead of names if your policy requires it.

plan.label: Ongoing
plan.title: Review the log once a month
plan.text: Count your referrals by type and by time of day. Compare the count with your team. Pick one replacement skill to teach next, and write it into the next report. Note what changed after you tried it.
